deepDive.title: Enzyme specificity and pH optima — why pepsin only works in your stomach
deepDive.body: In Class 7 you learned the stomach makes acid + enzymes. Class 8 introduces a crucial idea: each enzyme works at a SPECIFIC pH. Pepsin (stomach enzyme) works only in strong acid (pH 1.5-2.5). Pancreatic trypsin (small intestine) works only in mild alkali (pH 8). If you put pepsin in your small intestine, it would be inactive — wrong pH. This is why your digestive system is a SEQUENCE of distinct pH environments: mouth (pH 6.8), stomach (pH 2), small intestine (pH 8). Each region tuned for its specific enzymes. Drinking too much milk during indigestion — neutralises stomach acid, briefly disabling pepsin so the burning sensation fades. The enzymes resume working as acidity returns.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle after you're comfortable with stomach acid + digestive enzymes.
deepDive.nextStepHint: Class 11 introduces the active-site lock-and-key model — why an enzyme has ONE pH optimum.

deepDive.title: Villi math — why your small intestine is the size of a tennis court
deepDive.body: In Class 7 you learned villi are tiny finger-like projections in the small intestine. Class 10 makes the math concrete. Your small intestine is ~6 m long with diameter ~2.5 cm — surface area as a smooth tube would be only ~0.5 m². But the inside has CIRCULAR FOLDS (3× area = ~1.5 m²), each fold covered in VILLI 1 mm tall (10× = ~15 m²), each villus covered in MICROVILLI (20× = ~300 m²). Total absorptive surface: ~300 sq metres — the size of a tennis court folded into your abdomen. Why so much area? Speed: glucose, amino acids, fats need to be absorbed before food moves on. Surface area × diffusion rate = absorption capacity. Same math your skin avoids (which is why you can't absorb food through your hand — way too little surface area).
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle after the basic small-intestine concept.
deepDive.nextStepHint: Class 12 connects this to membrane biology — each microvillus is a tiny absorption machine.

deepDive.title: Hormonal control — gastrin, CCK, secretin
deepDive.body: Class 7 says: stomach makes acid 'when food arrives'. Class 11 reveals the messenger system. When you SEE/SMELL food, the brain signals vagus nerve → stomach starts releasing acid (yes, before any food arrives — that's why your mouth waters). When food TOUCHES the stomach lining, gastrin hormone is released → MORE acid + pepsin. When acid + food enter the duodenum, CCK (cholecystokinin) is released → gallbladder squeezes bile, pancreas releases enzymes. Simultaneously, SECRETIN tells the pancreas to release alkaline bicarbonate to neutralise stomach acid. The digestive system is a chemically-coordinated assembly line driven by hormones, not just nerve signals.
deepDive.nextStepHint: NEET tests every gut hormone, source, target, and effect — this Class 7 chapter is the entry point.
